If you're new to this wiki, begin with these three foundational pages:

  • mediterranean-diet — The complete overview: core principles, cardiovascular benefits, and clinical evidence
  • secondary-cardiovascular-prevention — How dietary intervention fits into post-MI care and long-term heart health
  • lyon-diet-heart-study — The landmark 1999 trial that showed a 50–70% reduction in recurrent cardiac events on a Mediterranean-style diet

docs.title: The Mediterranean Pattern
docs.text:
The traditional Mediterranean dietary pattern is the most extensively studied eating style for cardiovascular protection. Rooted in the food traditions of Greece, Italy, Southern France, Spain, and the Levant during the 1950s–1960s, it emphasizes whole plant foods, healthy fats, and minimal processed foods.

Core pillars:

  • extra-virgin-olive-oil — The primary fat source; rich in monounsaturated fatty acids and polyphenols that support endothelial function
  • Vegetables and Fruits — Daily staples, consumed in large quantities; provide potassium, fiber, and antioxidants
  • legumes — Beans, lentils, and chickpeas; eaten daily or several times per week as a plant-based protein source
  • whole-grains — Unprocessed cereals including wheat, barley, bulgur, and oats; the daily carbohydrate foundation
  • fish — Especially fatty fish (salmon, sardines, mackerel); the primary animal protein, rich in omega-3 fatty acids
  • Moderate cheese and wine — Cheese and yogurt as regular condiments; wine in low-to-moderate amounts with meals
  • Limited red-meat — Red meat is a few-times-per-month food, not a daily staple

Key foods not yet covered: mediterranean-herbs (parsley, basil, oregano, thyme, rosemary), poultry, eggs, cheese, yogurt, eggplant, tahini, canola-oil

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Understanding the biological mechanisms that drive Mediterranean diet benefits:

  • systemic-inflammation — Chronic low-grade inflammation drives atherosclerosis; the Med diet reduces inflammatory markers through polyphenols and omega-3 fatty acids
  • anti-inflammatory-environment — The physiological state promoted by Med diet fats (ALA, polyphenols) and food choices; counteracts inflammatory pathways
  • anti-thrombotic-environment — Med diet components (olive oil polyphenols, ALA, fish omega-3s) reduce platelet aggregation and thrombotic risk
  • blood-pressure-reduction — Achieved through increased potassium, magnesium, and fiber from vegetables and legumes; sodium reduction through herb-based seasoning
  • dyslipidemia-management — Mediterranean pattern improves the lipid profile: lowers triglycerides, raises HDL-C, and reduces atherogenic lipoprotein particles
  • plaque-regression — Evidence from Ornish trial shows intensive lifestyle change can reduce non-calcified plaque volume

docs.title: Supporting Nutrients and Biomarkers
docs.text:
• omega-3-fatty-acids — EPA and DHA from fish; ALA from canola oil and walnuts
  • alpha-linolenic-acid — Plant-based omega-3; the key cardioprotective nutrient in the Lyon study
  • lipoprotein-a — Lp(a), an independent ASCVD risk marker elevated in many post-MI patients
  • apolipoprotein-b — ApoB, the primary structural protein of atherogenic lipoprotein particles
  • sodium — Key target for reduction; Mediterranean cooking replaces salt with herbs, garlic, and lemon
  • potassium, magnesium, calcium — Electrolytes that support blood pressure regulation through vascular tone

docs.text:
Head-to-head analyses of dietary patterns, clinical formulas, and intervention strategies.

docs.title: Comparison of Formulas
docs.text: Formula Status Accuracy Best Use Case Martin/Hopkins Recommended by 2026-acc-aha-dyslipidemia-guidelines High General clinical practice Sampson/NIH Recommended by 2026-acc-aha-dyslipidemia-guidelines High Alternative when triglycerides are elevated Friedewald Legacy / Deprecated Moderate (underestimates at high TG) Historical reference only

docs.title: Why the Shift?
docs.text: The legacy Friedewald formula becomes increasingly inaccurate as triglyceride levels rise, often underestimating LDL-C. Modern equations account for variations in lipoprotein composition, providing more reliable data for dyslipidemia-management and risk-stratification.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text: Clinicians should transition to Martin/Hopkins or Sampson/NIH for all routine LDL-C estimation to ensure treatment decisions are based on accurate lipid quantification.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The ornish-lifestyle-heart-trial randomized patients with coronary atherosclerosis into an intensive lifestyle modification group versus a usual-care control group.

docs.title: Dimensions of Comparison
docs.text: Dimension Intensive Lifestyle Intervention Usual Care Diet very-low-fat-vegetarian-diet (~10% fat) Standard American Heart Association diet advice Exercise Moderate aerobic exercise No structured requirement Stress Management Yoga, meditation, group support None Plaque Change Stenosis decreased (regression) Stenosis progressed Angina Reduction 72% decrease in frequency Minimal change MACE Risk Significantly lower 2.47x higher risk ratio

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text: Intensive, multi-component lifestyle-modification can induce measurable plaque-regression and reduce clinical cardiac events compared to standard medical advice alone.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The lyon-diet-heart-study compared a Mediterranean-style dietary pattern against a "Prudent Western-type diet" for secondary prevention after myocardial infarction.

docs.title: Dimensions of Comparison
docs.text: Dimension Mediterranean-Style Diet Prudent Western Diet Fat Profile High in monounsaturated fats (olive oil), rich in alpha-linolenic-acid Higher in saturated fats, lower in omega-3s Food Quality Whole grains, legumes, fruits, vegetables More processed foods, refined carbohydrates Cardiac Events 50-70% reduction in recurrent MI and cardiac death Standard / higher event rate Mechanism Anti-inflammatory, anti-thrombotic Pro-inflammatory, standard atherogenic progression

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text: The Mediterranean-style diet dramatically outperforms the prudent Western diet in secondary cardiovascular prevention, primarily through non-lipid cardioprotective pathways.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Clinical and dietary concepts underpinning heart-healthy eating and post-MI recovery.

Browse individual topics in the sidebar, or use search to find specific concepts.

docs.title: Anti-inflammatory Environment
docs.text: An anti-inflammatory environment in the vasculature helps prevent the progression of atherosclerosis and the stabilization of plaques. Dietary patterns like the mediterranean-diet promote this environment through high intakes of antioxidants and omega-3-fatty-acids.

docs.title: Related Concepts
docs.text: Reducing systemic-inflammation is a primary mechanism through which anti-inflammatory environments are achieved.

docs.title: Anti-thrombotic Environment
docs.text: An anti-thrombotic environment reduces the likelihood of blood clot formation in the arteries, which is a primary cause of myocardial infarction. The lyon-diet-heart-study suggests that certain dietary patterns, including the mediterranean-diet, foster this environment.

docs.title: Blood Pressure Reduction
docs.text: The process of lowering systemic blood pressure through lifestyle and nutritional interventions. The Mediterranean diet — rich in vegetables, legumes, extra-virgin olive oil, nuts, and fish — is one of the most clinically proven dietary patterns for achieving sustainable blood pressure reduction. Key mechanisms include the anti-inflammatory and anti-thrombotic environments promoted by Mediterranean dietary fats (particularly alpha-linolenic-acid and polyphenols), increased potassium intake from vegetables and fruits, and reduced sodium from whole-food preparation.

docs.title: Dietary Sodium
docs.text: Achieving sustainable blood pressure reduction typically requires adherence to a low-sodium whole-food dietary pattern. Sodium targets for post-MI patients are detailed in clinical guidelines and should be individualized in consultation with a care team.

docs.title: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)
docs.text: The long-term, progressive loss of kidney function. The cordioprev-trial suggested that the mediterranean-diet might offer a kidney-protective effect, attenuating the decline of the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR).

docs.title: Dyslipidemia Management
docs.text: Dyslipidemia management involves the use of lifestyle modifications and lipid-lowering-therapy (like statin-therapy) to control abnormal lipid levels and reduce cardiovascular risk. The 2026-acc-aha-dyslipidemia-guidelines provides the current standard for this management.

docs.title: Assessment Tools
docs.text: Effective dyslipidemia-management requires accurate lipid quantification, covered under ldl-c-calculation-formulas, and evaluation of residual-risk-assessment after primary targets are met.

docs.title: Hypertension
docs.text: Hypertension (high blood pressure), typically defined as blood pressure greater than 130/90 mmHg, is a major cardiovascular disease risk factor. Each increment of 20 mmHg in systolic or 10 mmHg in diastolic doubles cardiovascular disease risk across the entire BP range from 115/75 to 185/115 mmHg. The Mediterranean diet has been shown to lower blood pressure through increased intake of potassium, magnesium, and fiber from vegetables, fruits, and legumes; the anti-inflammatory effects of extra-virgin-olive-oil polyphenols; and the anti-thrombotic environment promoted by alpha-linolenic-acid and omega-3 fatty acids from fish.

docs.title: Lifestyle Modification
docs.text: A broad term for changes in behavior and habits (diet, exercise, stress management) aimed at improving health outcomes. The ornish-lifestyle-heart-trial demonstrated that structured lifestyle modifications can be as effective as pharmacological interventions for certain outcomes like plaque-regression.

docs.title: Clinical Evidence
docs.text: The lifestyle-intervention-vs-usual-care comparison summarizes trial evidence for structured lifestyle programs versus standard care. secondary-cardiovascular-prevention frequently incorporates these modifications as a core pillar.

docs.title: Lipid-Lowering Therapy
docs.text: Lipid-lowering therapy (LLT) encompasses pharmacological and lifestyle interventions aimed at reducing atherogenic lipoproteins in the blood. The cornerstone of modern LLT is statin-therapy, though the 2026-acc-aha-dyslipidemia-guidelines also emphasize dyslipidemia-management through dietary patterns and risk-stratified targets.

docs.title: Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events (MACE)
docs.text: MACE is a composite endpoint used in clinical trials to measure the combined incidence of major cardiovascular events, such as myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, and cardiovascular death. The cordioprev-trial used this as a primary measure of efficacy.

docs.title: Plaque Regression
docs.text: Plaque regression is the reversal or reduction of atherosclerotic plaque buildup in the arteries. The ornish-lifestyle-heart-trial provided clinical evidence that intensive lifestyle-modification can achieve this, even in patients with severe coronary disease.

docs.title: Residual Risk Assessment
docs.text: Residual risk assessment involves identifying remaining cardiovascular risk in patients after they have achieved their primary lipid targets. Markers like apolipoprotein-b and lipoprotein-a are used to assess residual atherogenic and inflammatory risk.

docs.title: Risk Stratification
docs.text:
Risk stratification is the process of categorizing patients into different risk levels (e.g., low, intermediate, high, very high) to guide the intensity of dyslipidemia-management. The 2026-acc-aha-dyslipidemia-guidelines provides frameworks for this stratification.

The 2026-acc-aha-dyslipidemia-guidelines provide the primary clinical framework for cardiovascular risk stratification based on LDL-C thresholds and overall ASCVD risk.

docs.title: Secondary Cardiovascular Prevention
docs.text:
Secondary cardiovascular prevention refers to the medical and lifestyle interventions implemented after a patient has experienced an initial cardiovascular event (such as a myocardial infarction or stroke) to prevent recurrence. Key components include aggressive lipid management, blood pressure control, and nutritional strategies like the mediterranean-diet.

Beyond pharmacological management, intensive lifestyle-modification (as seen in the ornish-lifestyle-heart-trial) has also been shown to facilitate plaque-regression.

The cordioprev-trial provided additional evidence that a Mediterranean-style diet can reduce the risk of recurrent MACE compared to low-fat alternatives.

Modern guidelines, such as the 2026-acc-aha-dyslipidemia-guidelines, emphasize aggressive dyslipidemia-management and risk-stratification to reduce atherosclerotic-cardiovascular-disease.

docs.title: Related Interventions
docs.text:
• lifestyle-intervention-vs-usual-care: Evidence for intensive lifestyle changes.
  • systemic-inflammation: Inflammatory pathways that persist despite standard care.
  • residual-risk-assessment: Evaluating risk remaining after initial treatment.

docs.title: Sodium Reduction
docs.text: Reducing the intake of sodium is a primary strategy for managing hypertension and reducing cardiovascular risk. In the context of a Mediterranean-style dietary pattern, sodium reduction is achieved through emphasizing whole foods — vegetables, legumes, herbs, garlic, citrus, and vinegar — rather than processed or packaged foods. The Mediterranean diet's naturally low sodium profile, combined with its emphasis on extra-virgin olive oil as a primary fat source, supports both blood pressure control and arterial health.

docs.title: Systemic Inflammation
docs.text: Systemic inflammation is a key driver in the progression of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). Biomarkers such as high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) are used to monitor this state. Dietary patterns that reduce inflammation, such as the mediterranean-diet, are critical in managing long-term risk and promoting secondary-cardiovascular-prevention.

docs.title: 2026 ACC/AHA Dyslipidemia Guidelines
docs.text: The 2026 American College of Cardiology (ACC) and American Heart Association (AHA) Dyslipidemia Guidelines provide the current clinical standard for managing abnormal lipid levels and reducing cardiovascular risk. They recommend strict LDL-C treatment goals based on risk-stratification, universal screening for lipoprotein-a, and the use of apolipoprotein-b for residual atherogenic risk assessment. The guidelines explicitly recommend against using unregulated dietary supplements like fish oils and red yeast rice.

docs.title: Alpha-Linolenic Acid (ALA)
docs.text: Alpha-Linolenic Acid (ALA) is an essential omega-3 fatty acid. The lyon-diet-heart-study highlighted its role in cardioprotection, particularly when consumed as part of a mediterranean-diet. ALA is found in high concentrations in foods like flaxseeds, chia seeds, hemp hearts, and canola oil.

docs.title: Apolipoprotein B (ApoB)
docs.text:
Apolipoprotein B (ApoB) is a primary marker for atherogenic lipoproteins. The 2026-acc-aha-dyslipidemia-guidelines recommends using ApoB for a more accurate assessment of residual atherogenic risk than LDL-C alone.

The guidelines position ApoB as a key marker for residual atherogenic risk, often used alongside statin-therapy evaluation.

docs.title: Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease (ASCVD)
docs.text: Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease (ASCVD) is a spectrum of conditions caused by the buildup of plaque in the arteries. It is the target of both dyslipidemia-management and intensive secondary-cardiovascular-prevention.

docs.title: Calcium
docs.text: Calcium is essential for bone health and plays a vital role in blood pressure regulation. It is abundant in Mediterranean diet staples including leafy green vegetables, legumes, and dairy (when consumed).

docs.title: Canola Oil
docs.text: Canola oil (derived from rapeseed, bred for low erucic acid content) is a plant-based cooking oil notable for its high proportion of alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) — the plant-based omega-3 fatty acid. It was central to the lyon-diet-heart-study intervention, where butter and cream were entirely replaced with a canola-oil-based margarine supplied to participants.

docs.title: Nutritional Profile
docs.text:
• Fatty acid composition: Approximately 60% monounsaturated (oleic acid), 20% polyunsaturated (including 10% ALA), and 7% saturated fat
  • ALA content: Canola oil is among the richest common culinary oils in ALA (approximately 9–11%), making it a significant plant-based omega-3 source — particularly important in the Mediterranean context where alpha-linolenic-acid was the key cardioprotective nutrient in the Lyon study
  • Vitamin E: Contains tocopherol (natural antioxidant), protecting the oil and providing dietary vitamin E

docs.title: Role in the Lyon Diet Heart Study
docs.text:
The Lyon Diet Heart Study used a specialized canola-oil-based margarine as the primary fat source for the intervention group. This margarine was:

  • Comparable to olive oil in saturated fat (~15% of energy) and oleic acid (~48% of energy)
  • Uniquely rich in ALA at 4.8% — nearly 8x the ALA content of typical olive oil (0.6%)
  • Supplied exclusively to intervention participants to replace butter and cream

The intervention group experienced a 50–70% reduction in recurrent cardiac events compared to the control group. The authors attributed much of this benefit to the high ALA content of the canola-oil margarine, which promoted an anti-inflammatory-environment and anti-thrombotic-environment.

docs.title: Cardiovascular Evidence
docs.text:
• ALA (from canola oil, flaxseed, and walnuts) has been associated with reduced sudden cardiac death risk and lower rates of cardiovascular events in prospective cohorts
  • Replacing saturated fats with canola oil or other unsaturated oil blends reduces LDL-C and improves the total-to-HDL cholesterol ratio
  • The cardiovascular benefit of canola oil is primarily mediated through ALA content, polyphenol-independent mechanisms (unlike extra-virgin-olive-oil)

docs.title: Mediterranean Context
docs.text: Traditional Mediterranean cooking relied on olive oil rather than canola oil. Canola oil is not native to the Mediterranean basin; however, the Lyon Diet Heart Study demonstrated that a canola-oil-based spread could substitute for butter/cream in a Mediterranean-style pattern and still confer substantial cardioprotection. Canola oil is used in modern Mediterranean-style dietary approaches as a complement to — rather than replacement for — extra-virgin olive oil.

docs.title: Cheese
docs.text: Cheese is a fermented dairy product and a traditional source of protein and calcium in the Mediterranean diet. Traditional Mediterranean cheese varieties include feta (Greece), ricotta (Italy), manchego (Spain), and halloumi (Cyprus/Levant). Cheese is consumed in moderate amounts — typically as a condiment or dessert rather than a primary protein source.

docs.title: Nutritional Profile
docs.text: Cheese provides a combination of protein, calcium, phosphorus, and vitamin B12. Hard and semi-hard cheeses like parmesan and cheddar are particularly dense in these nutrients. Feta cheese — commonly used in Mediterranean salads and meze — is lower in fat than many hard cheeses and provides probiotics from the fermentation process.

docs.title: Cardiovascular Considerations
docs.text:
The relationship between cheese and cardiovascular health is nuanced:

  • Saturated fat: Cheese is high in saturated fat (approximately 20–25% of calories in most varieties), which has historically raised concerns for LDL-C elevation. However, emerging evidence suggests the food matrix structure of cheese may attenuate the cholesterol-raising effect compared to equivalent saturated fat from butter or processed meats
  • Calcium and potassium: The mineral density of cheese contributes to blood-pressure-reduction through electrolyte balance
  • Fermentation and probiotics: Fermented cheeses contain bioactive peptides and may support gut microbiome diversity, which is increasingly recognized in cardiovascular risk

docs.title: Mediterranean Role
docs.text: In the mediterranean-diet, cheese is consumed in moderate amounts — typically a few times per week rather than daily — and paired with vegetables, whole grains, and extra-virgin-olive-oil. The traditional Greek diet ( Crete, 1960s) included cheese primarily as feta in salads, yogurt as a breakfast staple, and small amounts of hard cheese as a seasoning.

docs.title: CORDIOPREV Trial
docs.text: The CORDIOPREV trial compared the efficacy of a Mediterranean diet against a low-fat diet in patients with coronary heart disease (CHD). The study found that the Mediterranean diet group had a 28.1% lower risk of recurrent major-adverse-cardiovascular-events (MACE).

docs.title: Additional Findings
docs.text:
• Kidney protection: The trial showed attenuated eGFR decline, relevant to chronic-kidney-disease.
  • Direct comparison: mediterranean-vs-low-fat-diet details the full dietary comparison.

docs.title: Eggplant
docs.text: Eggplant (Solanum melongena) is a nightshade vegetable native to the Indian subcontinent and naturalized across the Mediterranean. It is a staple in Greek, Italian, Turkish, Lebanese, and Egyptian cuisines — featured in dishes such as baba ganoush, moussaka, caponata, and imam bayaldi. Eggplant has a meaty texture and absorbs oils and sauces well, making it suitable for Mediterranean cooking methods that use extra-virgin-olive-oil.

docs.title: Nutritional Profile
docs.text: Eggplant is low in calories (approximately 25 kcal per 100g) and provides fiber, manganese, B6, folate, and polyphenols — notably nasunin, an anthocyanin pigment that gives the purple skin its color and acts as a potent antioxidant.

docs.title: Cardiovascular Properties
docs.text:
• Low sodium: Naturally very low in sodium, supporting sodium-reduction goals
  • Nasunin and polyphenols: Nasunin is a free-radical scavenger that protects cell membranes from oxidative damage, particularly relevant to vascular endothelial function
  • Fiber: The fiber content supports gut microbiome health and blood-pressure-reduction through short-chain fatty acid production
  • Low glycemic impact: Eggplant has a low glycemic index and is often paired with protein and fat in Mediterranean preparations, minimizing glucose spikes

docs.title: Mediterranean Culinary Uses
docs.text: In Mediterranean cuisine, eggplant is typically roasted, grilled, or fried in olive oil before being incorporated into dishes. Traditional preparation methods — such as scoring and salting eggplant before cooking to draw out bitter juices — reduce moisture and allow better oil absorption. Dishes like baba ganoush (smoky roasted eggplant with tahini and garlic) and Greek moussaka (layered eggplant with tomato and cheese) are central to the cuisine.

docs.title: Eggs
docs.text: Eggs are a versatile protein and nutrient-dense food consumed regularly across Mediterranean cultures. They are used in breakfasts (shakshuka, Greek spanakopita), baking, pasta, and as a binding agent in vegetable dishes. The Mediterranean approach to eggs is diverse — prepared by poaching, scrambling, hard-boiling, or baking with vegetables and herbs — and does not typically pair eggs with processed meats or high-saturated-fat accompaniments.

docs.title: Nutritional Profile
docs.text:
Eggs are one of the most nutrient-dense whole foods:

  • High-quality protein: Approximately 6g of protein per large egg, with a complete amino acid profile
  • Choline: Eggs are the richest dietary source of choline, important for neurological function and lipid transport (phosphatidylcholine)
  • B vitamins: B12, riboflavin (B2), and folate — particularly concentrated in the yolk
  • Vitamin D: Eggs contain vitamin D (approximately 40 IU per large egg), primarily in the yolk
  • Minerals: Selenium, iodine, iron, and phosphorus

docs.title: Cardiovascular Considerations
docs.text:
The relationship between egg consumption and cardiovascular risk has been extensively studied and is nuanced:

  • Dietary cholesterol: A large egg contains approximately 185 mg of cholesterol. For most individuals, dietary cholesterol has a modest effect on plasma LDL-C — the larger determinant is saturated fat intake
  • Replacing processed meats: In the Mediterranean dietary pattern, eggs serve as a protein source that replaces processed and red meats — a beneficial trade-off
  • The Ornish context: The Ornish Lifestyle Heart Trial allowed egg whites (no limit) but excluded yolks as part of its very-low-fat (<10%) vegetarian protocol, reflecting a more restrictive approach than Mediterranean dietary patterns

docs.title: Mediterranean Preparation
docs.text:
In traditional Mediterranean cooking, eggs are prepared:

  • Shakshuka: Eggs poached in spiced tomato and pepper sauce (North African, adopted in Mediterranean cuisine)
  • Spanakopita: Phyllo pastry with spinach and egg-based filling (Greek)
  • Frittata: Open-faced omelet with vegetables and herbs (Italian)
  • Huevos divorciados: Eggs with salsa and beans (Mexican influence; replaced with Mediterranean herbs and tomato in the wiki context)

docs.title: Extra-Virgin Olive Oil (EVOO)
docs.text: Extra-virgin olive oil is a staple of the mediterranean-diet and is highly valued for its unique profile of monounsaturated fatty acids and polyphenols. It was a key component in the cordioprev-trial.

docs.title: Fish
docs.text: Fish is a lean protein source emphasized in the Mediterranean diet. Fatty fish (such as salmon, mackerel, sardines, and tuna) are particularly valued for their high content of omega-3-fatty-acids, which support cardiovascular health and may reduce inflammation.

docs.title: Fruit
docs.text: Fruits are a foundational component of the Mediterranean diet, which emphasizes fruits as a primary plant-based food. Fruits provide essential potassium, fiber, vitamins, and antioxidants that support blood-pressure-reduction and overall cardiovascular health.

docs.title: Legumes
docs.text: Legumes—including beans, lentils, chickpeas, and peas—are plant-based protein sources foundational to the Mediterranean diet. They are rich in fiber, protein, and minerals while being low in saturated fat. The Mediterranean diet includes legumes daily or several times per week, providing plant-based protein alongside extra-virgin olive oil and vegetables.

docs.title: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)]
docs.text:
Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined lipoprotein that increases cardiovascular risk. The 2026-acc-aha-dyslipidemia-guidelines recommends universal screening for Lp(a) at least once in adulthood.

These guidelines provide the clinical framework for managing Lp(a)-related risk alongside dyslipidemia-management strategies.

docs.title: Lyon Diet Heart Study
docs.text: The Lyon Diet Heart Study was a landmark randomized trial that demonstrated a 50% to 70% reduction in recurrent myocardial infarction and cardiac death in patients following a Mediterranean-style diet. The study emphasized the importance of alpha-linolenic-acid and demonstrated cardioprotection through non-lipid pathways.

docs.title: Magnesium
docs.text: Magnesium is a mineral that supports various bodily functions, including muscle and nerve function and blood pressure regulation. It is abundant in leafy green vegetables, legumes, and nuts — all staples of the Mediterranean diet.

docs.title: Mediterranean Diet
docs.text: The Mediterranean diet is a dietary concept first proposed in 1975 by Ancel Keys and Margaret Keys, inspired by the eating habits of Greece, Italy, Southern France, Spain, and the Levant during the late 1950s to early 1960s. It is the most well-known and researched dietary pattern in the world.

docs.title: Core Principles
docs.text: The Mediterranean diet emphasizes: - Plant-based foods: Unprocessed cereals, legumes, vegetables, and fruits as dietary foundations - Healthy fats: extra-virgin-olive-oil as the principal source of fat, rich in monounsaturated fatty acids and polyphenols - Moderate protein: fish and dairy (mostly cheese and yogurt) in moderate amounts - Limited red meat: Low amounts of red meat, refined grains, and added sugars - Wine: Optional low to moderate consumption, typically with meals - Low saturated fat: High in monounsaturated fat and dietary fiber

docs.title: Cardiovascular Benefits
docs.text:
The Mediterranean diet is extensively studied for cardiovascular protection:

  • All-cause mortality: Associated with reduction in overall mortality in observational studies
  • Heart disease: 2017 review confirmed lowered risk of heart disease and early death
  • Stroke prevention: 2014 meta-analysis found elevated olive oil consumption specifically reduced stroke risk
  • Women's health: 2023 review demonstrated reduced mortality and CVD risk specifically in women
  • Cancer: 2021 review associated adherence with 13% lower risk of cancer mortality; strict adherence correlated with 6% decreased risk of dying from cancer
  • Cognitive health: 2013 systematic review found greater adherence correlated with lower risk of Alzheimer's disease and slower cognitive decline
  • Weight management: May help with weight loss in obese people through natural calorie reduction

docs.title: Recognition and Standards
docs.text: The Mediterranean diet is recognized by the World Health Organization as a healthy eating pattern and was designated an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in 2010.

docs.title: Clinical Evidence in Post-MI Recovery
docs.text: Significant benefits for secondary prevention were demonstrated in the lyon-diet-heart-study, which showed a 50–70% reduction in recurrent cardiac events when following this pattern, particularly through consumption of alpha-linolenic-acid. The cordioprev-trial further supported its efficacy, showing a 28.1% lower risk of recurrent major-adverse-cardiovascular-events compared to low-fat alternatives.

docs.title: Key Foods and Comparisons
docs.text:
• Core components: extra-virgin-olive-oil, tree-nuts, fatty fish, and whole grains
  • Compared to low-fat: mediterranean-vs-low-fat-diet
  • Compared to Western: mediterranean-vs-western-diet
  • Inflammation: Helps reduce systemic-inflammation through anti-inflammatory nutrients

docs.title: Mediterranean Herbs
docs.text: Mediterranean herbs are a defining characteristic of the culinary traditions of Greece, Italy, Southern France, Spain, and the Levant. They are used liberally — often dried and combined — to flavor foods without relying on salt, cream, or processed seasonings. Common Mediterranean herbs include parsley, basil, oregano, thyme, rosemary, sage, marjoram, and dill.

docs.title: Parsley (Petroselinum crispum)
docs.text: Parsley is the most widely used fresh herb in Mediterranean cooking. Rich in vitamin K, vitamin C, folate, and flavonoids (notably apigenin). It is used fresh in salads (tabbouleh), as a garnish, and in cooked dishes. Apigenin has demonstrated anti-inflammatory properties in cellular studies.

docs.title: Basil (Ocimum basilicum)
docs.text: A foundational herb in Italian and Greek cuisine, used in pestos, salads (caprese), and tomato-based sauces. Basil contains eugenol, linalool, and rosmarinic acid — compounds with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity.

docs.title: Oregano (Origanum vulgare)
docs.text: A strongly flavored dried herb in Greek and Turkish cuisine, used on grilled meats, in tomato sauces, and in salad dressings. Oregano is one of the most antioxidant-dense culinary herbs, particularly high in carvacrol and thymol, which have demonstrated antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties.

docs.title: Thyme (Thymus vulgaris)
docs.text: Used in Mediterranean meat, vegetable, and legume dishes. Thyme contains thymol and rosmarinic acid, both studied for their anti-inflammatory effects and contribution to the anti-inflammatory-environment.

docs.title: Rosemary (Rosmarinus officinalis)
docs.text: Common in Italian and Spanish cooking, rosemary contains rosmarinic acid, carnosol, and carnosic acid — compounds with strong antioxidant activity and preliminary evidence for cognitive health benefits.

docs.title: Mediterranean Role
docs.text: Herbs are used as the primary seasoning in Mediterranean cooking — replacing salt, butter, and cream. A typical Greek salad (horiatiki) uses parsley and oregano; an Italian basil and tomato sauce uses basil without any dairy or processed seasoning. The herb-and-vinegar or herb-and-lemon flavor profile is central to Mediterranean cuisine.

docs.title: Cardiovascular Connection
docs.text: The liberal use of herbs in Mediterranean cooking supports sodium-reduction by providing intense flavor without sodium. The polyphenolic compounds in herbs — including rosmarinic acid, eugenol, and apigenin — contribute to the overall anti-inflammatory polyphenol load of the Mediterranean dietary pattern, supporting endothelial function and the anti-thrombotic-environment.

docs.title: Nuts
docs.text: Nuts are nutrient-dense foods recommended in heart-healthy dietary patterns. The mediterranean-diet emphasizes nuts as a key component, and specific varieties like tree-nuts were featured in the cordioprev-trial. Nuts provide healthy unsaturated fats, protein, fiber, and micronutrients that support cardiovascular health. Replacing animal proteins with nuts and seeds may further reduce mortality risks.

docs.title: Omega-3 Fatty Acids
docs.text: Omega-3 fatty acids are a class of polyunsaturated fatty acids that are essential for cardiovascular health. They include alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). They contribute to an anti-inflammatory-environment and anti-thrombotic-environment.

docs.title: Ornish Lifestyle Heart Trial
docs.text: The Ornish Lifestyle Heart Trial was a landmark randomized, controlled clinical trial that demonstrated the ability of intensive, non-pharmacological lifestyle modifications to induce regression of coronary atherosclerosis. Key components included a very-low-fat-vegetarian-diet, aerobic exercise, stress management, and group support.

docs.title: Comparison Context
docs.text: The lifestyle-intervention-vs-usual-care page provides a structured comparison of the trial's intervention against standard medical care.

docs.title: Potassium
docs.text: Potassium is an essential mineral that helps regulate blood pressure by offsetting the effects of sodium and easing tension in blood vessel walls. It is abundant in vegetables, fruits, and legumes — key components of the Mediterranean diet.

docs.title: Poultry
docs.text: Poultry — chicken, turkey, and to a lesser extent duck and rabbit — is a lean protein source in the Mediterranean diet. It is consumed in moderate amounts and typically prepared by grilling, roasting, or braising with herbs, garlic, and olive oil, rather than by deep-frying.

docs.title: Nutritional Profile
docs.text:
Poultry is lower in saturated fat than red meat and provides:

  • High-quality protein: Approximately 25–30g of protein per 100g serving
  • B vitamins: Niacin (B3), pyridoxine (B6), and B12 — supporting energy metabolism and neurological function
  • Low saturated fat: Skinless chicken breast contains approximately 3–4% fat, of which only a fraction is saturated
  • Minerals: Phosphorus, selenium, and zinc

docs.title: Mediterranean Role
docs.text:
The mediterranean-diet pattern emphasizes poultry as a preferred alternative to red meat. The lyon-diet-heart-study explicitly replaced red meat with poultry in the intervention group, limiting beef, pork, and lamb while increasing fish and chicken intake.

Poultry is prepared in Mediterranean cuisine in several characteristic ways:

  • Grilled with herbs: Chicken souvlaki (skewered, grilled with olive oil, lemon, and oregano)
  • Roasted with vegetables: Chicken baked with tomatoes, olives, and capers (类皮达尔式)
  • Braised in tomato-based sauces: Turkey or chicken legs braised with peppers, onions, and Mediterranean herbs

docs.title: Cardiovascular Considerations
docs.text: Swapping poultry for red meat in the Mediterranean pattern contributes to lower saturated fat intake and supports the lipid profile goals of secondary-cardiovascular-prevention. However, processed poultry (e.g., breaded chicken nuggets, deli turkey slices) is not equivalent to whole cuts — processed forms introduce sodium and added fats that undermine the cardiovascular benefit.

docs.title: Red Meat
docs.text: Red meat (beef, pork, lamb) is limited in the Mediterranean diet due to its high saturated fat content. The Mediterranean diet specifically limits red meat in favor of fish, poultry, and plant-based proteins. High consumption of red meat (>14g/day) and processed red meat has been associated with cardiovascular death.

docs.title: Sodium
docs.text: Sodium is a mineral that plays a key role in fluid balance. However, high sodium intake is strongly linked to increased blood pressure. In a Mediterranean-style dietary pattern, sodium reduction is achieved through cooking with herbs, garlic, citrus, and vinegar rather than added salt, and by avoiding processed and packaged foods.

docs.title: Sourdough Bread
docs.text:
Sourdough bread is bread leavened through natural fermentation by wild yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae wild strains) and lactic acid bacteria (Lactobacillus species) rather than commercial baker's yeast. This ancient method, originating in Egypt around 1500 BC, produces a bread with distinct nutritional and metabolic properties relevant to cardiovascular health.

Unlike conventional bread, the sourdough fermentation process modifies the starch structure, reduces antinutrients, and generates bioactive compounds that confer heart-protective benefits beyond those of standard whole-grain bread.

docs.title: Lower Glycemic Response
docs.text:
Sourdough bread has a substantially lower glycemic index (GI ~54) compared to conventional white bread (GI ~70–85) and even many whole-wheat breads. This is attributed to:

  • Lactic acid fermentation altering the structure of starch molecules, slowing carbohydrate digestion and glucose absorption
  • Organic acids (lactic and acetic acid) produced during fermentation inhibiting starch gelatinization and reducing the rate of starch hydrolysis
  • Lower postprandial insulin response — multiple studies show participants eating sourdough bread have lower blood sugar and insulin spikes than those eating baker's-yeast bread

For secondary-cardiovascular-prevention, maintaining stable blood glucose is important because postprandial hyperglycemia drives oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and systemic inflammation — all contributors to atherosclerosis progression.

docs.title: Improved Mineral Bioavailability
docs.text:
Whole grains contain phytate, an antinutrient that binds minerals and reduces absorption. Sourdough fermentation reduces phytate content by over 70% through the action of lactic acid bacteria, which lower the dough pH and activate endogenous phytase enzymes. This significantly increases the bioavailability of:

  • Potassium — essential for blood pressure regulation and vascular tone
  • Magnesium — supports endothelial function and arrhythmia prevention
  • Calcium — involved in vascular smooth muscle contraction
  • Zinc and iron — important for immune function and oxygen transport

These minerals directly support the blood-pressure-reduction mechanisms central to Mediterranean dietary patterns.

docs.title: Prebiotic Effect and Short-Chain Fatty Acid Production
docs.text:
Sourdough fermentation produces prebiotic compounds — indigestible oligosaccharides and resistant starch — that serve as fuel for beneficial gut bacteria. Colonic fermentation of these prebiotics generates short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), particularly:

  • Butyrate: The primary energy source for colonocytes; emerging research shows butyrate has positive inotropic effects on cardiac muscle and reduces systemic inflammation through epigenetic regulation
  • Acetate and propionate: Modulate lipid metabolism, reduce hepatic cholesterol synthesis, and improve insulin sensitivity

A 2024 human trial (Da Ros et al.) demonstrated that sourdough consumption significantly raised butyrate and acetate levels in the gut compared to conventional bread, with anti-inflammatory effects observed across 40 healthy volunteers. The gut-heart axis is increasingly recognized as a mediator of cardiovascular risk.

docs.title: Enhanced Antioxidant Activity
docs.text:
The lactic acid bacteria in sourdough increase the availability of phenolic compounds and other antioxidants during fermentation. These antioxidants:

  • Protect LDL particles from oxidative modification — a key step in atherogenesis
  • Reduce systemic-inflammation markers including C-reactive protein
  • Support endothelial nitric oxide production, promoting vasodilation

Peptides generated during sourdough fermentation have demonstrated antioxidant properties in vitro that may lower risk for chronic diseases including cardiovascular disease.

docs.title: Lower Gluten Content
docs.text: The acidic environment of sourdough fermentation partially degrades gluten proteins, making the bread easier to digest for individuals with mild gluten sensitivity. This may support dietary adherence — a critical factor in long-term lifestyle-modification for post-MI patients. Note: Sourdough is NOT suitable for celiac disease; residual gluten remains.

docs.title: Mediterranean Context
docs.text:
Traditional bread throughout the Mediterranean region was historically made with natural levain — essentially a sourdough process — long before commercial yeast became available. In the traditional Mediterranean dietary pattern:

  • Bread was consumed daily as a vehicle for extra-virgin-olive-oil, vegetables, and legumes
  • Whole-grain sourdough loaves provided sustained energy without sharp glycemic spikes
  • The lyon-diet-heart-study emphasized bread as a daily staple in the Mediterranean intervention group

The synergy between sourdough's lower GI, improved mineral absorption, and prebiotic effects aligns closely with the dietary principles underlying cardiovascular protection.

docs.title: Research Highlights
docs.text:
• A randomized controlled trial (2024, preprint) investigating sourdough bread in metabolic syndrome found trends toward improved glycemic control and reduced inflammatory markers compared to conventional bread
  • Sourdough fermentation reduces phytate content by more than 70% at optimal pH (4.3–4.6) and temperature (25°C)
  • Multiple cross-over studies demonstrate lower postprandial glucose and insulin responses to sourdough versus baker's-yeast bread
  • The Da Ros et al. human trial (2024) confirmed that sourdough consumption significantly increases gut SCFA (butyrate, acetate) production compared to conventional bread
  • 2025 research (Springer) demonstrated anti-inflammatory and antioxidant potential of sourdough extracts in vitro

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
• Choose true sourdough: Many commercial "sourdough" breads use baker's yeast with added acidulants for flavor — they do not provide the same benefits. Look for bread made with live sourdough starter (ingredient lists should show only flour, water, salt, and starter)
  • Prefer whole-grain: While sourdough improves the nutrition of any flour, whole-grain sourdough provides more fiber, minerals, and antioxidants than refined-flour versions
  • Pair with Mediterranean fats: Enjoy with extra-virgin-olive-oil for dipping, alongside legumes and vegetables — following the traditional Mediterranean pattern
  • Moderation: As with all bread, sourdough is calorically dense. One to two servings daily aligns with the Mediterranean pattern
  • Not gluten-free: Individuals with celiac disease should avoid wheat, barley, or rye sourdough

docs.title: Statin Therapy
docs.text: Statin therapy is a cornerstone of dyslipidemia-management and secondary-cardiovascular-prevention, primarily used to lower LDL-C and reduce the risk of atherosclerotic-cardiovascular-disease.

docs.title: Tahini
docs.text: Tahini is a paste made from ground, roasted sesame seeds. It is a cornerstone of Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cuisine, used in baba ganoush, hummus, halva, and as a condiment for grilled vegetables and flatbreads. It provides a concentrated source of植物油 derived fat with a distinctive nutty flavor.

docs.title: Nutritional Profile
docs.text:
Tahini is energy-dense (approximately 600 kcal per 100g) but nutrient-rich:

  • Healthy fats: Approximately 50–60% fat, predominantly unsaturated — with a favorable ratio of monounsaturated (MUFAs) to polyunsaturated (PUFAs) fatty acids
  • Plant-based protein: About 20% protein by weight, providing amino acids complementary to legume proteins
  • Minerals: Very high in phosphorus, magnesium, manganese, iron, and zinc — nutrients often low in Western diets
  • B vitamins: Contains B1 (thiamine), B3 (niacin), and B6

docs.title: Cardiovascular Properties
docs.text:
• Unsaturated fat profile: Replaces saturated fats when used as a spread or condiment instead of butter or cream
  • Phytosterols: Sesame seeds contain phytosterols (notably beta-sitosterol), which compete with cholesterol for intestinal absorption and support healthy lipid profiles
  • Sesamin and sesamolin: These lignans found in sesame seeds have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, supporting the anti-inflammatory-environment of the Mediterranean dietary pattern
  • Magnesium: Tahini is an excellent source of magnesium, supporting muscle and nerve function and blood pressure regulation

docs.title: Mediterranean Culinary Context
docs.text: In the Mediterranean and broader Eastern Mediterranean region, tahini is used as a sauce base (mixed with lemon juice and garlic over roasted vegetables), as a spread on bread, and as a component of desserts. Traditional preparations use raw or lightly roasted sesame seeds, and the paste can be made at home or purchased pre-ground.

docs.title: Tree Nuts
docs.text: Tree nuts are a significant source of healthy fats and micronutrients. They are emphasized in dietary patterns like the mediterranean-diet and were part of the nutritional intervention in the cordioprev-trial.

docs.title: Vegetable
docs.text: Vegetables are a cornerstone of the Mediterranean diet, which emphasizes vegetables as a foundational plant-based food. Vegetables are rich in potassium, magnesium, fiber, and antioxidants with minimal caloric density, making them ideal for weight management and cardiovascular protection.

docs.title: Very Low-Fat Vegetarian Diet
docs.text: A dietary pattern characterized by extremely low fat intake and a focus on whole plant foods. This was the cornerstone of the ornish-lifestyle-heart-trial and was shown to contribute to plaque-regression.

docs.title: Whole Grains
docs.text: Whole grains are cereal grains consumed in their complete form — bran, germ, and endosperm intact — making them a foundational component of the mediterranean-diet. Common varieties include wheat, barley, oats, bulgur, farro, spelt, and whole-grain pasta and bread. Naturally leavened sourdough-bread — made through wild yeast and lactic acid fermentation — offers additional cardiovascular benefits beyond standard whole-grain bread, including a lower glycemic index and improved mineral bioavailability.

docs.title: Cardiovascular Benefits
docs.text:
Whole grains are strongly associated with cardiovascular protection through multiple mechanisms:

  • Fiber and beta-glucan: Soluble fiber, particularly beta-glucan in oats and barley, reduces LDL-C by binding bile acids and increasing fecal excretion
  • Blood pressure reduction: Regular whole grain consumption is associated with lower systolic and diastolic blood pressure
  • Inflammation reduction: Whole grains reduce systemic inflammation markers including CRP
  • Glycemic control: Low glycemic index whole grains reduce postprandial glucose spikes, supporting weight management and insulin sensitivity
  • Gut microbiome: Fermentation of whole grain fiber produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that support arterial health

docs.title: Mediterranean Context
docs.text: The traditional Mediterranean dietary pattern emphasizes unprocessed cereals — primarily as bread, bulgur, and whole-grain porridges — as a daily staple. These are consumed with olive oil, legumes, and vegetables rather than with butter, cream, or processed meats.

docs.title: Research Highlights
docs.text:
• A 2016 meta-analysis of 45 studies found that 3 servings of whole grains daily reduced cardiovascular disease risk by 20–30%
  • The lyon-diet-heart-study emphasized bread as a primary component of the Mediterranean intervention group, consumed daily alongside vegetables, fish, and fruit
  • Whole grains are a key component of the anti-inflammatory-environment promoted by the Mediterranean dietary pattern

docs.title: Wine
docs.text: Wine — specifically red wine — is a traditional component of the Mediterranean diet, consumed in low to moderate amounts with meals, typically during social occasions and family dinners. The traditional Mediterranean pattern does not emphasize heavy drinking; rather, it uses wine as an accompaniment to food, generally consumed with the main meal rather than on an empty stomach.

docs.title: Polyphenol Content
docs.text:
Red wine is a significant source of polyphenols — particularly resveratrol, anthocyanins, catechins, and quercetin — derived from grape skins and seeds during fermentation. These compounds have been extensively studied for their antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.

Key polyphenols in red wine: - Resveratrol: A stilbenoid studied for its effects on SIRT1 activation, cellular stress resistance, and inflammation reduction. Found in the skin of red grapes; concentrated in red wine due to extended skin contact during fermentation - Anthocyanins: Pigment compounds that give red wine its color; associated with improved endothelial function - Catechins and proanthocyanidins: Condensed tannins from grape seeds with antioxidant activity

docs.title: Cardiovascular Evidence
docs.text:
A U-shaped (J-shaped) relationship between alcohol consumption and cardiovascular outcomes has been consistently observed:

  • Moderate consumption (approximately 1 drink per day for women, 1–2 for men): associated with 20–40% lower cardiovascular risk compared to non-drinkers and heavy drinkers in large prospective cohorts
  • Heavy consumption: associated with increased risk of hypertension, atrial fibrillation, stroke, and heart failure
  • The cardioprotective effect of moderate wine consumption is attributed to polyphenol-mediated improvements in endothelial function, anti-inflammatory effects, and modest HDL-C elevation

docs.title: Mediterranean Context
docs.text: In the traditional Mediterranean pattern (Crete, 1960s), wine was consumed daily with meals — typically at lunch and dinner — in amounts of 1–3 glasses per day for adult men. The pattern emphasized food-first consumption (never on an empty stomach) and was integrated into a broader lifestyle of physical activity, social meals, and minimal processed food.

docs.title: Clinical Considerations
docs.text:
• The 2026-acc-aha-dyslipidemia-guidelines and prior guidelines acknowledge moderate alcohol consumption as an individual consideration within overall dietary patterns
  • Wine is not recommended as a cardioprotective strategy for non-drinkers (the risk of initiating alcohol use outweighs uncertain benefits)
  • Individuals with a history of atrial fibrillation, liver disease, or certain medications should avoid alcohol entirely
  • The Mediterranean diet without wine remains cardioprotective, as demonstrated by the Lyon Diet Heart Study, which did not include alcohol recommendations

docs.title: Yogurt
docs.text: Yogurt is a fermented dairy product made by culturing milk with beneficial bacteria (primarily Lactobacillus and Streptococcus species). It is a traditional component of the Mediterranean diet, particularly in Greece and the Levant, where it is consumed as a breakfast food, a sauce base (tzatziki), or a snack with nuts and fruit.

docs.title: Nutritional Profile
docs.text: Yogurt provides high-quality protein, calcium, potassium, and B vitamins. Greek yogurt — strained to remove whey — has approximately double the protein content of conventional yogurt per serving. Plain, unsweetened yogurt is preferred in the Mediterranean context; sweetened or flavored varieties introduce added sugars that are otherwise minimized.

docs.title: Cardiovascular and Metabolic Benefits
docs.text:
The fermented nature of yogurt provides benefits beyond its basic nutritional content:

  • Probiotic effects: Yogurt contains live cultures that support gut microbiome diversity. A healthy gut microbiome is associated with reduced systemic-inflammation and improved lipid profiles
  • Blood pressure reduction: The combination of potassium, calcium, and probiotic peptides in yogurt has been associated with modest reductions in systolic blood pressure
  • Glycemic control: Yogurt consumption is associated with improved insulin sensitivity and lower postprandial glucose, supporting weight management
  • Calcium and blood-pressure-reduction: Like cheese, yogurt provides calcium and potassium in a format that supports electrolyte balance and vascular health

docs.title: Mediterranean Context
docs.text: In the traditional Mediterranean diet, full-fat plain yogurt was a common breakfast item, often served with honey, nuts, or figs. Modern Mediterranean dietary recommendations support regular consumption of plain yogurt as part of the dairy component, emphasizing whole-food preparation over sweetened varieties.

title: Air Fryer Chicken Wings with Lemon Pepper Sauce description: Golden-crispy chicken wings tossed in a warm lemon pepper butter sauce — a crowd-pleasing appetizer or main that comes together in 30 minutes with a short prep and a 20-minute air fryer cook. The sauce uses a homemade lemon pepper blend with fresh lemon zest and honey. author: Lisa Bryan source: https://downshiftology.com/recipes/air-fryer-chicken-wings/ rating: 5.0 review_count: 26 recipe_yield: 4 prep_time_minutes: 10 cook_time_minutes: 20 total_time_minutes: 30 servings: 2 cuisine: Mediterranean-inspired category: Air Fryer equipment: - Air Fryer - Small saucepan - Small bowl tags: - poultry - air-fryer - quick - high-protein - game-day keywords: - air fryer chicken wings - lemon pepper wings - crispy wings ingredients: - 1 pound chicken wingettes and drummettes (about 10 wings), patted dry - 1 tbsp extra virgin olive oil - 1 tbsp lemon pepper seasoning - 1/2 tsp kosher salt - For the sauce: - 4 tbsp unsalted butter, melted (or ghee for dairy-free) - 1 tbsp honey - 1 tsp finely grated lemon zest - 1.5 tbsp fresh lemon juice (from half a lemon) - 1 tsp lemon pepper seasoning - 1/2 tsp garlic powder instructions: - Preheat the air fryer to 390°F (200°C) for 2–3 minutes. - Pat the chicken wings completely dry with paper towels. Drying the skin is critical for maximum crisping. - In a bowl, toss the wings with olive oil, lemon pepper seasoning, and salt until evenly coated. - Place the wings in a single layer in the air fryer basket (work in batches if needed). Stir well and warm over low heat for 2–3 minutes until the honey has dissolved and the sauce is smooth. - Transfer the hot wings to a large bowl. docs.text:
title: Air Fryer Falafel with Tahini Sauce description: Crispy, herb-packed falafel made entirely in the air fryer — no deep frying required. The falafel mixture (soaked chickpeas, parsley, cilantro, garlic, warm spices) is shaped and air fried to golden perfection, served with a simple tahini-lemon sauce. Authentic technique, modern appliance. author: Lisa Bryan source: https://downshiftology.com/recipes/falafel/ rating: 4.94 review_count: 508 recipe_yield: 18 prep_time_minutes: 60 cook_time_minutes: 15 total_time_minutes: 75 servings: 3 cuisine: Mediterranean / Middle Eastern category: Air Fryer equipment: - Air fryer - Food processor - Large bowl tags: - legumes - air-fryer - vegetarian - vegan - high-protein - make-ahead keywords: - falafel - air fryer falafel - chickpea falafel - tahini sauce - Mediterranean appetizer ingredients: - For the falafel: - 1 cup dried chickpeas, soaked overnight in plenty of cold water (do not use canned) - 1/2 cup roughly chopped onion - 1 cup roughly chopped parsley (about 1 large bunch) - 1 cup roughly chopped cilantro (about 1 large bunch) - 1 small green chile pepper (serrano or jalapeño) - 3 garlic cloves - 1 tsp ground cumin - 1 tsp salt - 1/2 tsp ground cardamom - 1/4 tsp black pepper - 2 tbsp chickpea flour (or plain flour) - 1/2 tsp baking soda - For the tahini sauce: - 1/4 cup tahini - 2 tbsp fresh lemon juice - 1 small garlic clove, minced - 2–4 tbsp cold water (to thin) - 1/4 tsp salt - Pinch of cumin - For cooking: - Olive oil or avocado oil spray instructions: - Soak the chickpeas: Place dried chickpeas in a large bowl, cover with plenty of cold water (they will triple in size), and soak for at least 8–12 hours or overnight. Drain and rinse well before using. (This step cannot be rushed or skipped — unsoaked chickpeas will not blend properly and the falafel will be gritty.) - Make the falafel mixture: Add the soaked chickpeas, onion, parsley, cilantro, garlic, green chile, cumin, salt, cardamom, and black pepper to a food processor. Pulse in short bursts, scraping down the sides as needed, until the mixture resembles coarse sand — not smooth hummus, but a chunky, workable texture. Do not over-blend. - Chill the mixture: Transfer the falafel mixture to a bowl. Stir in the chickpea flour and baking soda. Cover and refrigerate for 30 minutes to 1 hour. This resting time helps the mixture hold its shape during cooking. - Shape the falafel: Use your hands, an ice cream scoop, or a falafel scoop to form the mixture into balls or small patties (about 1.5 inches in diameter). If the mixture is too wet to hold, add another tablespoon of chickpea flour. If it's too dry and crumbly, add a teaspoon or two of water. - Air fry: Preheat the air fryer to 375°F (190°C). Lightly spray the falafel with olive oil or avocado oil spray on all sides. Place them in a single layer in the air fryer basket (work in batches — about 6–8 at a time). Air fry for 10–12 minutes, flipping halfway through, until deep golden and crispy on all sides. - Make the tahini sauce: While the falafel cook, whisk together the tahini, lemon juice, garlic, salt, and cumin in a small bowl. Add cold water a tablespoon at a time, whisking constantly, until you reach a smooth, pourable consistency (about the texture of heavy cream). - Serve: Arrange the hot falafel on a platter, drizzle with tahini sauce, and garnish with a sprinkle of paprika and fresh parsley. Serve with warm pita, a simple salad, or on its own as a protein-rich snack. nutrition_per_serving: calories: 310 fat_g: 14 saturated_fat_g: 2 carbohydrates_g: 36 fiber_g: 9 sugar_g: 5 protein_g: 13 cholesterol_mg: 0 sodium_mg: 490 potassium_mg: 540 nutrition_note: Based on 3 servings of 6 falafel each. Nutrition includes falafel only; tahini sauce adds approximately 90 calories and 8g fat per 2-tablespoon serving. The soaking step requires passive time but no active work — plan ahead. why_this_recipe_fits: | Chickpeas (legumes) are a foundational food in the Mediterranean pattern — featured in CORDIOPREV and every traditional Mediterranean diet. Falafel delivers 13g of protein and 9g of fiber per serving, making it one of the most filling plant-based options available. The air fryer produces the same crispy result as deep frying with a fraction of the oil (1–2 teaspoons vs. a full pot of oil). Tahini adds phytosterols and sesamin/sesamolin lignans that support cardiovascular health. wikilinks: - legumes - tahini - mediterranean-herbs related_recipes: - everyday-mediterranean-salad - air-fryer-salmon-capers

Falafel is one of the great success stories of Mediterranean cuisine — a plant-powered, protein-rich food that travels from the Levant to every corner of the world. This version uses the air fryer to achieve the signature crispy exterior without deep frying, making it approachable for a weeknight dinner.

The key to great falafel is the overnight soak (plan ahead) and the coarse texture in the food processor. Don't blend it smooth — you're looking for a mixture that holds together but still has visible herb flecks. The tahini sauce takes 3 minutes and transforms the dish from good to exceptional.

title: Air Fryer Mediterranean Salmon with Capers description: Crispy-edged, tender salmon fillets finished with capers, lemon, and herbs in just 20 minutes — no marinade needed. The air fryer delivers restaurant-quality texture with minimal active time and almost no cleanup. author: Lisa Bryan source: https://downshiftology.com/recipes/air-fryer-salmon/ rating: 5.0 review_count: 135 recipe_yield: 4 prep_time_minutes: 5 cook_time_minutes: 15 total_time_minutes: 20 servings: 2 cuisine: Mediterranean category: Air Fryer equipment: - Air fryer - Small bowl tags: - fish - air-fryer - quick - high-protein - keto-friendly - pescatarian keywords: - air fryer salmon - Mediterranean salmon - salmon with capers - lemon salmon ingredients: - 4 (6-ounce) salmon fillets, patted very dry - 2 tbsp Dijon mustard - 1 tsp sweet paprika - 1 tsp garlic powder - 1/2 tsp kosher salt - 1/4 tsp freshly ground black pepper - 1 tbsp extra virgin olive oil - 2 tbsp capers, drained - 1 lemon, thinly sliced - 1 tbsp fresh parsley, chopped - 1 tbsp fresh dill, chopped (optional) instructions: - Preheat your air fryer to 400°F (200°C) for 2–3 minutes. The air fryer is the weeknight secret weapon for a 50-year-old man who wants fast, high-quality protein without the cleanup. Four ingredients in the basket, 15 minutes, and a result that rivals a properly pan-seared restaurant salmon. The Dijon-paprika rub forms a golden, slightly caramelized crust while the interior stays flaky and moist.

The burst of capers and fresh lemon slices at the end give this dish its Mediterranean identity — no heavy sauces, no breading, just clean, bold flavors from olive oil, fish, and herbs.

Performance & Longevity Formula

docs.title: Why This Fits a Heart-Healthy Diet
docs.text:
While this shake extends beyond traditional Mediterranean fare, each component contributes to cardiovascular and metabolic health in ways that align with the wiki's dietary principles:

  • Extra-Virgin Olive Oil (EVOO): The polyphenols — specifically oleocanthal — help reduce systemic-inflammation and improve blood vessel elasticity. EVOO is the cornerstone fat of the mediterranean-diet and was central to the cordioprev-trial.

  • Omega-3 fatty acids from chia seeds and hemp hearts: These contribute to an anti-inflammatory-environment and help regulate triglycerides. Chia seeds are particularly rich in alpha-linolenic-acid (ALA), the plant-based omega-3 shown to reduce recurrent cardiac events in the lyon-diet-heart-study.

  • Fruit (berries, banana): Blueberries and blackberries supply vitamin C — essential for collagen synthesis — and anthocyanins that support endothelial function. Bananas provide potassium for blood-pressure-reduction.

  • Yogurt: Provides probiotics, calcium, and potassium — supporting gut microbiome diversity and modest blood pressure reduction.

  • Soluble fiber from psyllium husk, chia, and fruit: Supports healthy cholesterol excretion via bile acid binding — a mechanism discussed in dyslipidemia-management.

  • Creatine: While not a traditional Mediterranean ingredient, creatine supplementation has been studied for post-myocardial infarction cardiac function — it supports myocardial energy metabolism and ATP regeneration, which may aid recovery in a post-MI context.

  • Whey and collagen protein: Provide the amino acids glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline that are structural substrates for connective tissue repair and vascular wall integrity.

title: Greek Green Beans (Fasolakia Lathera) description: Tender green beans slow-stewed with tomatoes, onion, garlic, and extra virgin olive oil in the Greek tradition — a simple, wholesome one-pot dinner that tastes better the next day. The name "lathera" means "with oil," reflecting the olive oil–forward technique central to Mediterranean cooking. author: Elena Paravantes, MS, RD source: https://www.olivetomato.com/recipe/greek-green-beans-fasolakia/ rating: 5.0 review_count: 73 recipe_yield: 4 prep_time_minutes: 15 cook_time_minutes: 45 total_time_minutes: 60 servings: 2 cuisine: Greek category: Stove Top — One Pot equipment: - Large pot or Dutch oven with lid tags: - vegetables - one-pot - vegetarian - vegan - budget-friendly - meal-prep keywords: - fasolakia - Greek green beans - lathera - Greek green beans with tomato - spanakoria ingredients: - 1.5 pounds fresh green beans, trimmed (or frozen green beans, partially thawed) - 3 tbsp extra virgin olive oil (plus more for finishing) - 1 large yellow onion, diced - 3–4 garlic cloves, minced - 1 (14-ounce) can diced tomatoes (or 2 large fresh tomatoes, diced) - 1/2 cup tomato sauce - 1 tsp sweet paprika - 1/2 tsp ground cumin - 1/2 tsp salt (or to taste) - 1/4 tsp freshly ground black pepper - Pinch of red pepper flakes (optional) - 1/4 cup water - 1 tbsp fresh dill or parsley, chopped (for finishing) - Juice of half a lemon (optional, for brightness) instructions: - If using fresh green beans, trim the ends and cut them into 2-inch pieces. If the beans are very long, you can leave them whole — they will shrink as they cook. Set aside. - Heat the olive oil in a large pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and lightly golden — about 6–8 minutes. - Add the garlic, paprika, cumin, salt, pepper, and red pepper flakes. Stir for 30 seconds until the spices are fragrant. - Add the diced tomatoes, tomato sauce, and 1/4 cup of water. Stir well to combine and bring to a gentle simmer. - Add the green beans and toss to coat them in the sauce. The beans should be mostly submerged or at least well-coated. - Reduce the heat to low, cover the pot, and let the beans simmer for 35–45 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beans are very tender and the tomato sauce has thickened and caramelized slightly around the edges. - Check at the 30-minute mark. If there is too much liquid, uncover and let it reduce for a few minutes. If it's too dry, add a splash of water. - Taste and adjust the seasoning — the beans should be deeply savory, slightly sweet from the tomatoes, and fragrant with the spices. - Finish with a squeeze of lemon juice (if using), a drizzle of extra virgin olive oil, and a scattering of fresh dill or parsley. This is the kind of dish that defines what "Mediterranean cooking" actually looks like in a Greek home — not a composed restaurant plate, but a pot of vegetables slowly transformed by time, olive oil, and low heat into something deeply savory and satisfying.

Fasolakia Lathera is traditionally served at room temperature, making it an excellent meal prep candidate: cook a big pot on Sunday, portion it out for easy lunches and dinners across the week. The green beans absorb the tomato sauce as they cook, becoming tender without losing their character entirely.

Shakshuka is a beloved one-skillet dish across the Mediterranean and Middle East — eggs poached directly in a chunky, spiced tomato and bell pepper sauce. For a 50-year-old man looking for quick, heart-healthy dinners, it checks every box: one pot, 40 minutes, high protein, and built on an olive oil foundation with vegetables as the base.

The sauce leans on warm spices (coriander, paprika, cumin) that are common across Greek, Tunisian, and Egyptian kitchens. Finished with fresh parsley and a hint of mint, it's bright and satisfying without being heavy. Serve straight from the skillet at the table.
